課程綱要.課程目標: In the course, students will expect to: 1) Develop a critical understanding of the ways in which emotional literacy interacts with the popular culture via mass media, 2) Participate in various in-class presentations (individual and group) and sharpen their public speaking skills and 3) Develop analytic/ argumentative skills via various projects and in-class discussions
課程綱要.授課內容:
*本課程預設為英文系大一選修課程。非該設定範圍的學生計劃選修本課程(含英文系其他年級與外系)，請出席第一週的課程說明會(A-116)，並於課程結束後與授課老師聯繫。密碼卡將根據屆時的人數來決定發放。本課使用英語授課，所有的課堂討論與作業亦是以英文進行。
Starting as a debate in the field of philosophy on the interplay between human emotions and cognition on the eve of the millennium, the topic of emotions/affect began to receive considerable attention among critics across disciplines. With the increase in interdisciplinary conversations at the beginning of the twenty-first century—including neuroscience, cognitive psychology, political science, history, and literature—scholars have declared that we are now in the era of emotions. This course offers a platform for students to familiarize themselves with this trend by introducing the concept of “emotional literacy” (how do we “read” emotions) and its complicated, at times problematic, integrations with popular culture. Our course seeks to answer the following core questions: What is the nature of emotions? What role do they play in contemporary popular culture, particularly at the juncture of public opinion formation and censorship? This course consists of regular (short) lectures, group discussions, and movie screenings based on weekly assigned texts. The course will be conducted entirely in English, and no prerequisites are required.

課程綱要.課程目標: This course aims to introduce critical approaches to the study of modernity in relation to colonial histories. Its goal is to equip students with critical knowledges and analytical skills: 1) to examine how (Anglo-European) modernity is represented as a universalized teleology of historical progress for all humanity; 2) to develop decolonial perspectives of reconsidering our historical relationship to the colonial formations of modernity in the mediated everyday life by our social practices, political ideas, economic life, and cultural expressions. This introductory course gives students an understanding of the historical conditions out of which the English department has developed in non-Anglophone societies and is designed to prepare students with essential knowledge and skills for critical Anglophone studies in the department.
課程綱要.授課內容: Over the course of the semester, students will read select literary and cultural texts on colonialism from different historical periods and social perspectives. Students will also read excerpts from influential cultural theory on the colonial formations of modernity, and will be asked to apply this theory to the texts. Students will be expected to complete assigned readings before class, and be prepared to discuss the readings in group activities.

課程綱要.課程目標: 課程目標： Reading fiction as critique Working through concepts with historiographic contexts Writing with thought in motion
課程綱要.授課內容: This course will introduce a range of fiction from and critical writing on two settler colonial sites through its literatures in English, in Southern Africa of the post-war Apartheid era (Themba, Gordimer) and in US America of the pre-war early twentieth century (Larsen). Critical works we will read include histories (Feinstein, Thompson), political historiography and decolonial methodology (Mamdani), psychosocial theorization (Fanon), literary and cultural criticism (Piles, etc). The class will be conducted as an undergraduate seminar, with an emphasis on close reading, in-class discussions and organic writing. We will read works of fiction alongside critical essays (from a Gaoguan reader) that situate these works as part of an early international-ist northern American and southern African literature in English that critically think through what it means to mediate, or represent, stories of entangled relationships, in life, love, struggles and survival via published (public) writing, in settler colonial states with bifurcated modes of rule (Mahmood Mamdani). The works include: Native Life in South Africa (Sol [Solomon Tshekisho] Plaatje, 1916), Requiem for Sophiatown (Can Themba, 1924-1968, 2006), Occasion for Loving (Nadine Gordimer, 1960, 1963), July’s People (Nadine Gordimer, 1981), Quicksand and Passing (Nella Larsen, 1928, 1929). Those interested in taking the class could read Native Life in South Africa, Occasion for Loving and Quicksand during winter break. Required fiction will be made available through ee-class; a reader can be picked up at Gaoguan by January 31.

課程綱要.課程目標: “In the course, students will expect  To develop a critical understanding of the ways in which Arthurian literature came into being and became popular in the Middle Ages  To examine the ways in which Arthurian literature contributes to the making of European psyche  Develop critical thinking and argumentative skills via various in-class discussions and projects  To cultivate and enhance the skill set of research in the realm of literary and cultural studies“
課程綱要.授課內容:
*本課程系統設定為英文系大二選修課程。非此設定範圍但欲選修該課程的同學(含英文系其他年級及外系)，網路初選會被系統自動排除。如想要修課需參與開學第一堂課，並在課後與授課老師面談。若符合修課標準，會視情況核發選課密碼卡。
*This course is capped for sophomore English majors during course pre-registration period. For those who are not in this category but wish to take the course, you MUST attend the first class.
Since his first appearance in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s The History of Kings of Britain, King Arthur (as a literary figure) has gained high, unending popularity in the corpus of secular literature throughout the Middle Ages. In our survey we will read a cluster of medieval Arthurian texts that helps establish this very literary canon. As Arthurian literature (sometimes known as ‘Arthuriana’) remains a trans-European phenomenon, we will incorporate many texts outside of the Anglophone world in translation, and the chosen texts are roughly grouped under three linguistic headings: the Latin tradition (Geoffrey of Monmouth), the French tradition (Beroul and Chrétien de Troyes), and the English tradition (Marie de France, Chaucer, and Malory). By reading these texts, students are expected to not only gain a more diverse, comprehensive understanding of the changing nature of Arthurian legends, but also develop a critical sense of individual texts pertaining to their historical backgrounds and contexts. In addition, in order to frame Arthurian literature according to our modern concerns, we will spend a certain amount of time investigating themes pertaining to cultural colonialism, gender, emotion studies, and reception studies. The course will be conducted entirely in English and is open for all majors. Former knowledge of British Literature 1 is preferred.

課程綱要.課程目標: This course introduces students to the rise of the English novel, which is roughly coeval with the rise of the British colonial empire, industrial capitalism, and the middle class. We will examine a wide variety of novels (and some film adaptations), analyzing how their narrative form enables the construction of stories that reflect on and reinforce the development of middle-class values. In other words, we will consider how novels shape ostensibly progressive notions such as romantic individualism and female autonomy, as well as how they collude with repressive (sexual) mores, capitalist ideologies, and empire-building. Adopting a roughly chronological order, we will go over the Romantic, Victorian, and Modernist periods. Special emphasis will be placed on the way aesthetic forms are treated as means to carry out ethical practices that are not necessarily fully intentional. By closely engaging with the ambivalence or conflicts surrounding these aesthetic/ethical projects, students are expected to develop a more critical and historical understanding of the rise of English literary culture on the global stage and how it has shaped what are now understood to be Western values.
課程綱要.授課內容:
The class will consist of lectures and group discussions followed by groups reporting back to the class. There will be unannounced quizzes. Students are expected to complete assigned readings before each class meeting.
Novels are long, and we will only be able to read excerpts in this survey course, not the full novels. Surveys are meant to familiarize students with a field as a whole rather than looking closely at a few texts.
If time allows over the break, students are encouraged to read some of the novels in full (Chinese translation is fine) before class begins.
In class, all our readings will be in English. Novels we cover are likely to include Pride and Prejudice, Frankenstein (1818 version), Great Expectations, Heart of Darkness, Things Fall Apart, Lord of the Rings (novel excerpts and film trilogy), and The Remains of the Day (novel excerpts and film).

課程綱要.課程目標: This course is aimed at introducing how to develop linguistic observations into workable linguistic research ideas and proposals. Each week we will discuss one popular linguistic topic. Through discussing assigned topics, students will learn about these findings, theories and the significances, locate references with keywords, narrow observations into research questions and devise methods that answer research questions. By the end of the term, students are expected to work in groups or pairs to present a research proposal with solid support from known studies.

課程綱要.課程目標: “In this introductory course, we’ll address key issues and concerns as well as recent developments in comparative literature. We will do this by using affect, a.k.a. emotion, as the main conceptual fulcrum to bring together all of the literary and cultural texts to be studied in this semester. In the first few weeks, we will cover some of the seminal texts in the field, with a strong emphasis on the Chinese studies segment. We’ll then specifically tackle our concern about affect by examining how emotions could be felt or represented quite differently in East and West. In the first unit of our foray into affect, we will discuss questions such as: “Does an individual exist in a communitarian culture like ours?”; or “How does our community affect our feelings and thoughts?” The next three units will attempt to answer these questions by each looking at a different type of emotion. Unit B employs Jin Yong’s martial arts novel to consider how tragic pathos could occur in a literary tradition without a generic equivalent to Greek or Renaissance tragedies and how such tragic pathos might in fact be mediated by two contradictory forces: a Westernized notion of the tragic hero and an ambivalent attachment to communitarian ideals such as filial piety and patriotism. Shifting the analytic lens from literary to filmic texts, Unit C focuses on how female bodies have been coded as sources of terror in both Hollywood and Japanese horror films, and how a certain communitarian rejection of individuated feelings might have played into the logic of a Japanese gothic work like Ju-on （《咒怨》）. In our last comparative exercise, we will seek to understand how depressive feelings could be transferred or lost in translation, as we map out a trajectory wherein writers such as Ha Jin and Eileen Chang whose native language is not English nevertheless end up using English to describe characters’ feelings in the Chinese context, as something inextricably bound up with their kinship or community ties.“

課程綱要.課程目標: This theory and practice-based course seeks to provide students with conceptual and practical tools for motivating the act of translation, reassessing prevalent binaries in conceptualizing translation, translation as a public service and projects of foreignization, translation, and mediation that involve inter/intra relations of languages, mediums, forms and fields. To do so, we will weigh in on relevant theoretical resources by exemplifying the practice of translation.
課程綱要.授課內容: This course provides students with relevant concepts, techniques, and materials in performing translation tasks. Through lectures and guided discussions, we will work with real-world texts taken from translations of different genres and topics, including news and media reportage, ads and commercials, fiction and humor in films, websites and games, etc. Students will have opportunities to participate in a project and adapt texts and media to multilingual and multicultural environments. The purpose is to expand students‘ awareness of various ways of approaching translation.

課程綱要.課程目標: The objective is to strengthen students’ skills in argumentation and research writing. We will cover two interrelated areas: (1) argumentation and interpretation (structure in academic writing, interpretation techniques, logical argumentation vs. fallacies, definition of terms, anticipating counterarguments); and (2) using secondary sources (avoiding plagiarism, locating sources, note-taking techniques, drafting, strategies for incorporating secondary sources to strengthen, not lose, your own argument, language and sentence structures for lead-ins and analyses of secondary sources, MLA style documentation, annotated bibliography, literature review). These are skills necessary for writing research papers at the graduate level and in writing the MA thesis and thesis proposal.
課程綱要.授課內容:
The first assignments are textbook readings on structure and research methodology for academic essays in the humanities, and we will discuss these assignments by analyzing sample student papers. Each week students will be asked to write a short analysis of the structure and argumentation of a sample paper according to its use of one or more of the techniques introduced in the textbooks. Students will be assigned to go over the readings in class, leading a class discussion in which other students will actively participate.
During the second part of the course, our meetings will be conducted as workshop seminars also led by students. Each week, students will lead discussions of one or two papers written by other students taking this course. Each student will eventually submit at least one paper for this purpose and lead at least one discussion of a classmate’s paper. Although there will be designated discussion leaders, all students will be expected to prepare brief written feedback for each paper and participate in the discussions. These workshop discussions will be based on writing techniques covered in the first part of the semester. The final paper will be a revision of the workshop paper in response to the material covered in this course and feedback received during workshop. Critique will be rigorous but also very constructive (with emphasis on the latter), and students are expected to substantially rewrite their papers (not simply add a paragraph or two, but conduct further research, rethink and rewrite). In addition, each student will write an annotated bibliography to include five entries on articles or book chapters in their field of research. These secondary sources will be incorporated into students’ final, rewritten papers.
課程綱要.教科書/參考書: MLA Handbook, current edition, and Course Reader (at gaoguan).
課程綱要.授課方式: 研討 實習/實驗
課程綱要.評量配分比重: 1. Weekly writing/feedback assignments and participation in workshop discussions: 30% 2. Annotated bibliography: 20% 3. Rewritten final paper (with original paper, revision plan, outline and feedback sheets): 50% Please note: both poor attendance and plagiarism are grounds for failing the course.

課程綱要.課程目標: The course, with an interdisciplinary approach, explores how contemporary society understand poverty and represent the poor. By focusing on the intersection of poverty and culture, the course examines how sociologists use culture as a framework to understand and address poverty. We will look at how institutions, such as family, education, and neoliberal government, shape and intervene in the lives of the poor.
課程綱要.授課內容: In light of the research done and the knowledge produced in sociology, we will read poverty narratives in popular culture, particularly in the form of literary journalism, memoir, and autobiography, and explore how life narratives and individual experiences (re)shape our understanding of poverty and the poor and (re)configure our relations with the social margin. In relation to poverty narratives, the course is concerned about how upward social mobility is perceived, pursued, and achieved by individuals in life narratives. It explores how such stories of success contribute to specific knowledge about poverty and the poor, and examines how they either help or hinder the public’s understanding of the scope of the issue. We will also look at how social immobility or downward social mobility is conceived and narrated in the narratives of the homeless and the working poor to unravel the myth of social mobility. In doing so, the course attempts to explore the possibility of reconfiguring our responses to poverty and impoverished individuals.

課程綱要.課程目標: The primary objective of this course is to situate the study of poetic forms in comparative contexts, whether this be across languages (comparing, for instance, Chinese lyric poems to English ones) or across media (exploring poetic language in cinema, theatre, and even certain prose forms). Students will be tasked with developing a descriptive vocabulary that enables them to identify different types of poetic discourse when looking at individual poems, the broader works of a single author, and then in the comparative contexts suggested above.
課程綱要.授課內容:
Week 1: What is Comparative Poetics?
Introductory discussion and in-class group assignment.
Week 2: The Problem of Poetic Ontology
Lecture on the nature of literary production, authorship, dissemination, and the constitution of intended audiences.
Weeks 3-4: Ancient Theories of Poetic Genre
Readings and discussion from Aristotle, Schlegel, Hegel
Weeks 5-6: Medieval/Renaissance Theories of Poetic Genre
Readings and discussion from Dante and related secondary readings
Weeks 7-8: Modern Theories of Poetic Genre
Readings and discussion on the modern lyric (from Lyric Theory textbook)
Weeks 9-10: Poetics and Cinema
Movie screenings and discussions
Weeks 11-12: Poetics and Theatre
Readings and discussions of theories of Tragedy and Comedy, farce and satire, across time and space
Weeks 13-14: Poetics and the Novel
Readings from key modern novels and discussion.
Weeks 15-16: Presentations and Final Paper Preparation
課程綱要.教科書/參考書: The primary teaching materials will be poetic works from across the Western Canon, selected to catalyze students’ attention to the plurality of poetic discourses and their different poetic ontologies (epic, lyric, elegy, free verse, occasional poetry, propagandistic songs, folk songs, etc.). These will be accompanied by a range of poetic comparanda, such as movies that incorporate poetic elements in both cinematic terms and in their scripts (e.g. Wim Wenders Der Himmel uber Berlin, Wong Kar-Wai 2046) and by extracts from prose works often lauded for their poetic styles (e.g. Vladimir Nabokov Lolita, Virginia Woolf The Waves).
課程綱要.授課方式: 研討
課程綱要.評量配分比重: Students will be tasked with a midterm assignment and a final paper (respectively 20% and 30% of the final grade). The rest of the grade will be determined based on in-class activities, discussions, presentations, and overall attendance/participation.

課程綱要.課程目標: 完成課程時，學生應該達成以下目標： • 能辨識重要研究議問題和綜合現有文獻，來評估理論和實踐； • 能透過公共活動參與或社群媒體討論，來分析相關資料； • 能應用社會語言學、修辭學和/或言談分析等相關方法，來規劃和展示研究。
課程綱要.授課內容: 本課程探討流行文化和公共空間中的語言溝通和與修辭策略。課程融合社會語言學、批判性言談、數位傳播寫作、超語翻譯等多元研究視角，促進學生對相關文本的批判性思考及研討。討論聚焦數位環境的言談，以及其如何影響受眾和傳播思想，尤其是在社群媒體上，以及數位修辭在促進社會互動和行動方面的作用。除了全球英語的研究領域外，我們還將關注多語言和多模態的社群媒體言談，包括公共演講、數位敘事、政府宣傳、流行音樂、廣告創譯、新聞報導和網路迷因等。學生將綜合現有文獻進行研究，並展示研究成果。
